015ebc0087.note: The stem now gives Lind's own 'as similar as I could have them' (sportsci.org transcription: 'Their cases were as similar as I could have them'), so the key no longer rests on a premise only the context held. The 'mildest cases' choice stays live and wrong: picking cases alike does not show they were, and the other five pairs say nothing about the fruit pair's start. The dead any-fresh-fruit choice is gone; 'the oranges alone' is wrong because the pair ate oranges and a lemon together, so no pair could split them. Berth, diet, pairs, remedies, six days to fit for duty: all as Lind wrote.

6875a74ce8.note: Fact error fixed: Lind wrote 'Two of the worst patients, with the tendons in the ham quite rigid (a symptom none of the rest had)', so 'tendons behind the knee' is right. Old tell fixed: no stem clause about stopping the choosing remains, and the key is no longer Semmelweis's turn-taking point. Choice wording and length: 52 / 42 / 51 / 52 characters, so the key does not stand out by length. The key is the only hedged choice ('on average') and 'alike in every way' is the absolute one, but that absolute is the real misconception (randomisation makes the groups equal), and the context rebuts it with Grokipedia's 'probabilistic allocation rather than guaranteed equality'. The other two still need knowledge. The random-sampling choice is truly wrong here: the stem's 'the choice' is plainly which patient gets which remedy (assignment), and Grokipedia (Random assignment) separates assignment, which allocates 'participants already included in a study', from sampling, which makes a sample stand for a population. The blinding choice is wrong. Grokipedia: matching 'addresses known variables but fails to control for unknown or unmeasured confounders'. The 1948 streptomycin sealed envelopes, with Hill 'helped design', is accurate.

5a0d6b6403.note: The 'Yet' sentence is now in the context, so the stem no longer tells the player that Lind missed the modern lesson. The new line is right. JLL: in the third edition (1772) Lind wrote that lemon juice gave the most quick and sensible relief, 'by which I have relieved many hundred patients'. He was Chief Physician at Haslar from 1758 to 1783. It makes the diet-lack and fruit-only choices live lures. The key holds: in 1772 he still named 'improper diet, air and confinement' as causes (JLL); Wikipedia: salt meat in a damp atmosphere. The boiled-syrup choice is wrong, since Lind made the rob believing it kept its power. The context ends on the nature-of-science point the judge asked for.

09a68fc8d3.note: Only the context changed. Dimond, Kittle and Crockett (Kansas City, Am J Cardiol 1960;5:483-486) compared the ligation with a sham operation, and neither the cardiologists nor the patients knew which had been done. Miller (2012) says the 1959 and 1960 trials showed the ligation 'no better than a sham'. So the line is true, and the key no longer rests on 17 patients alone. The overlap with the T4 Mesmer key is unchanged and low, as the judge ruled.

fe74e5e255.note: Clarity fixed: the 1,082 is gone, and 'Set beside the dummy-pill patients' says what the needed group is compared with. Key and choices unchanged and right: only a group given nothing separates the dummy's own effect from natural recovery and regression to the mean (Wikipedia, Placebo; Kienle and Kiene 1997). An open-label dummy group still takes a pill, so it does not show this either. Known low cross-leak: ec890ef658's stem ('others got no treatment at all') hints at this key if a player meets it first; that is not new and was ruled low.

ec890ef658.note: Convergence fixed: the choices are now an even 2 x 2 grid (small or large, felt or measured), so every choice shares a part with exactly two others. Key right: in the 2001 review placebo had a small effect on continuous subjective outcomes, pain included (27 pain trials, SMD -0.27), and no significant effect on objective outcomes (SMD -0.12, CI crossing zero). So 'small effects on what tests measured' is wrong as the review's finding. The context now attributes the finding to the review and says the size is still argued (the stance fix).

b5592d97ec.note: Old tell fixed: the 83 percent is now the key's fact, not stem data. Cummings et al. (JAMA 2000, abstract via Europe PMC): of the alendronate women whose hip BMD fell more than 4 percent in year one, 83 percent (CI 82-84) gained in year two, a mean of 4.7 percent; those who gained 8 percent or more lost about 1 percent next. On the hand-over: the stem gives two premises, that most women gain and that each scan carries chance error. The student must still see that women picked for an extreme loss were mostly ordinary gainers misread, and that is the regression step most people get wrong. 'Another loss about as large' (these are the women the medicine fails; 'most' leaves room for them) and 'A smaller loss' (half a swing back) stay strong lures, so the premises do not hand over the conclusion. Context nit, not a fail: 'scans that had read low by chance' could read 'scans that had read wrong by chance', since a high first scan gives the same false loss.

ca6813493b.note: Clarity fixed: 'a sham, a fake exchange' glosses the term, and the long sentence is split. Facts unchanged and right (Noseworthy et al., Neurology 1994: each patient seen by a blinded and an unblinded neurologist; only the unblinded scores showed an apparent benefit for the plasma-exchange group). Overlap ruling: this keys the Noseworthy trial's assessor bias, measured directly, not the T4 Clever Hans fact (a questioner cueing his subject), the Franklin fact or the Emily Rosa fact.

72abaf6135.note: Rates right (Francis 1955, Table 3): 57 per 100,000 placebo, 16 vaccinated. The context's numbers hold: 500 x 57/100,000 = 0.29 cases, 500 x 16/100,000 = 0.08. The chance of no case at all is about 57 percent even with no vaccine effect and about 69 percent with it, so 'the likeliest outcome however well the vaccine worked' is true. ARITHMETIC RULING: allowed. It is an order-of-magnitude step done in the head (57 in 100,000 is under 1 in 1,000), the choices hold no numbers, and the point is the science one, that cases decide; it is not a maths-bank sum. Overlap fixed: the key is no longer the bare T3 one-seed or T4 small-groups-swing idea; it needs the expected count of a rare outcome. The lures are live misreadings: vaccine failed, polio absent (wrong: most infections never paralyse, and zero paralytic cases was expected anyway), children immune. Mild form note: the key is the only choice not starting 'That'. Optional parallel wording: 'That it proves nothing, as so few cases were to be expected'. Not a fail.

ace5f447a7.note: Fact error fixed. Francis Table 7 gives 72 percent (lower limit 61) for all paralytic cases in the placebo areas, which is 1 - 16/57. His 80 to 90 percent is 'the composite results against laboratory confirmed cases of paralytic poliomyelitis'. The context now says both, in that order. The stem's new sentence is right: in Table 3, observed areas, the second-grade not inoculated ran 35 per 100,000 (43 cases) against 46 (330 cases) for the first- and third-grade controls, and Francis says the refused second-graders 'also had a lower rate'. So the data now rule out the dummy shot as the cause of both gaps, without outside knowledge. The 'vaccinated elsewhere' choice, which the stem struck, is replaced. The new 'weak dose' choice is wrong by the rates themselves, since a weak vaccine would have lowered the dummy group's rate. That is reasoning, not a stem clause. 'Chance alone' is wrong: 115 and 121 cases, and two gaps in the same direction in two designs. The key alone explains both gaps.
